\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Classical price families for computing the degeneracy profile of a subset-sum instance at the production weight scale $a_i = O(n^{2})$. Rows list the exact dynamic-programming count, the SSG stored-record footprint, and the enumeration algorithms - meet-in-the-middle, Howgrave-Graham and Joux, and the quantum-walk variant. Entries are closed-form resource scalings from the cited analyses, with the record footprint taken from the retention law $\bar m \approx 3.7\,\|H\|\sqrt{\tau}$ measured in ED-N1r. The table supports the benchmark framing: lattice-priced methods pay in the spectral width $\|H\|$, enumeration-priced methods pay in $2^{cn}$ and matter only when the weights make the lattice exponentially wide, and at production scale dynamic programming is exact and polynomial. The record footprint rides the lattice axis as a consistency statement, not an advantage claim, and the table establishes no separation between SSG and classical methods and no hardness statement about subset-sum.}
\label{tab:dp-price}
\begin{ruledtabular}
\begin{tabular}{llll}
\textbf{Method} & \textbf{Price family} & \textbf{Leading-order scaling} & \textbf{Regime where the price binds} \\ \hline
Dynamic programming (Bellman table) & lattice & $n\,\|H\|$ & exact and polynomial at the production weight scale $a_i = O(n^2)$ \\
SSG stored record & lattice & $\bar m \approx 3.7\,\|H\|\sqrt{\tau}$ & the same axis - a consistency statement, not an advantage claim \\
Meet-in-the-middle & enumeration & $2^{n/2}$ & weights exponentially wide in $n$ \\
Howgrave-Graham and Joux & enumeration & $2^{0.337n}$ & weights exponentially wide in $n$ \\
Quantum walk & enumeration & $2^{0.216n}$ & weights exponentially wide in $n$ \\
\end{tabular}
\end{ruledtabular}
\end{table}
